procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 27.07.2017 of the High Court of Judicature at Madras in CRLRC No. 1268 of 2016.  Specifically, the High Court's order setting aside the charge framed by the Sessions Court against Respondent No. 2.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Respondent No. 2 filed an application under Section 227 Cr.P.C to get discharged from the case, which was dismissed. After the Sessions Court framed charges, Respondent No. 2 filed another application under Section 216 Cr.P.C. seeking modification of the charge. This application was also dismissed by the Sessions Court. Respondent No. 2 then preferred a Revisional Application (Crl.R.C. No. 1268 of 2016) before the High Court under Section 397 Cr.P.C challenging the Sessions Court's dismissal of the modification application. The High Court allowed the Revision Application and set aside the charge framed by the Sessions Court against Respondent No. 2.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant (presumably the original complainant or the state) appealed to the Supreme Court because the High Court's order was considered illegal, untenable, and dehors the material on record. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and restored the order passed by the Sessions Court. The Supreme Court also imposed a cost of Rs. 50,000 on Respondent No. 2 for derailing the proceedings with frivolous applications.

directions: The order passed by the High Court is set aside.
The order passed by the Sessions Court is restored.
A cost of Rs. 50,000/- is to be paid by the accused to the appellant.

issue.issue_text: Whether an accused has the right to file a fresh application under Section 216 of the Cr.P.C. seeking discharge after a charge has been framed, particularly when a previous discharge application under Section 227 of the Cr.P.C. has already been dismissed.

facts: The accused first filed an application for discharge from a murder trial under Section 227 of the Cr.P.C.
This application was dismissed by the Sessions Court, and the dismissal was upheld by the High Court.
Subsequently, the Sessions Court framed charges against the accused.
The accused then filed a new, 'vexatious' application under Section 216 of the Cr.P.C., seeking alteration of the charge, which was effectively another attempt to be discharged.
The Sessions Court dismissed this second application.
However, on a revision application filed by the accused, the High Court allowed the plea and discharged the accused.
law: Section 216 of the Cr.P.C. is an enabling provision that gives the *court* the power to alter or add to any charge at any time before a judgment is pronounced.
Section 216 does not grant any right to the *accused* to file a fresh application seeking discharge after a charge has already been framed.
An order dismissing an application to modify a charge under Section 216 is an interlocutory order.
Under Section 397(2) of the Cr.P.C., a revision application against an interlocutory order is not maintainable.
application: The Supreme Court found that the accused, having already failed to get discharged under Section 227, was misusing the legal process by filing another application under Section 216.
The Court characterized this second application as a 'vexatious' attempt to 'derail the criminal proceedings.'
It clarified that the power under Section 216 belongs to the court and is not a tool for the accused to re-argue for discharge after the appropriate stage (under Section 227) has passed.

Furthermore, the Court held that the High Court should not have even considered the revision application. The Sessions Court's order dismissing the Section 216 application was an interlocutory order, and a revision against it was expressly barred by law.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the accused's contention, holding that an accused has no right to file a fresh application under Section 216 of the Cr.P.C. to seek discharge after a charge has been framed, particularly when a previous discharge application under Section 227 has already been considered and dismissed. Such a practice was deemed deplorable and an abuse of the legal process.

issue.issue_text: Whether a revision application under Section 397 of the Cr.P.C. is maintainable against an order that dismisses an application seeking modification of a charge.

facts: An accused's application to modify a charge under Section 216 of the Cr.P.C. was dismissed by the Sessions Court.
The accused then challenged this dismissal by filing a revision application under Section 397 of the Cr.P.C. before the High Court.
law: Section 397(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) contains an express bar prohibiting courts from exercising revisional jurisdiction over interlocutory orders.
application: The Supreme Court classified the trial court's order, which dismissed the application to modify the charge, as an "interlocutory order."
Because the order is interlocutory, it falls directly under the prohibition established in Section 397(2) of the Cr.P.C.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the revision application was not maintainable. The express bar in Section 397(2) of the Cr.P.C. prevents a revision application from being filed against an interlocutory order, and an order dismissing an application to modify a charge is such an order.

issue.issue_text: What is the scope of interference and exercise of revisional jurisdiction under Section 397 of the Cr.P.C. against an order framing a charge.

law.law_text: The scope of revisional jurisdiction under Section 397 of the Cr.P.C. is extremely limited and should be exercised very sparingly, not in a routine manner.
Section 397(2) of the Cr.P.C. expressly prohibits a court from exercising revisional powers against an interim or interlocutory order.

Even when revision is permissible under Section 397(1), it is only meant to correct a patent defect or an error of jurisdiction or law. Interference is justified only if the lower court's decision is grossly erroneous, there is non-compliance with the law, the finding is based on no evidence, material evidence is ignored, or judicial discretion is exercised arbitrarily or perversely.

application.application_text: The Court classified an order dismissing an application for modification of a charge (under Section 216 Cr.P.C.) as an interlocutory order.
Applying the legal bar from Section 397(2), the Court determined that since the order related to framing a charge is interlocutory, a revision application against it is not maintainable.

The Court emphasized that a revisional court must be "extremely circumspect" when reviewing an order framing a charge and should be reluctant to interfere unless the case substantially falls within the narrow categories justifying intervention (e.g., being grossly erroneous or perverse).

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court decided that the scope of interference under Section 397 Cr.P.C. with an order framing a charge is extremely limited. It held that such an order is interlocutory in nature, and therefore, a revision is barred by Section 397(2). Even in cases where revision is considered, a higher court should only interfere sparingly and in exceptional circumstances, such as when the trial court's order is grossly erroneous, perverse, based on no evidence, or an arbitrary exercise of discretion.

arguments.issue_text: Whether an accused has the right to file a fresh application under Section 216 of the Cr.P.C. seeking discharge after a charge has been framed, particularly when a previous discharge application under Section 227 of the Cr.P.C. has already been dismissed.
appellant_arguments: The accused was misusing the process of law by filing frivolous and untenable applications one after another to derail the proceedings.
respondent_arguments: The accused had a right to file an application seeking modification of the charge even after a prior discharge application was dismissed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a revision application under Section 397 of the Cr.P.C. is maintainable against an order that dismisses an application seeking modification of a charge.
appellant_arguments: An order dismissing an application for modification of a charge is an interlocutory order.
Due to the express bar in Section 397(2) of the Cr.P.C., a revision application against such an interlocutory order is not maintainable.
respondent_arguments: The revision application was maintainable against the order dismissing the application for modification of the charge.

arguments.issue_text: What is the scope of interference and exercise of revisional jurisdiction under Section 397 of the Cr.P.C. against an order framing a charge.
appellant_arguments: The High Court exceeded its revisional jurisdiction by setting aside the charge framed by the Sessions Court.
The High Court's order was ex facie illegal, untenable, and contrary to the material on record, ignoring settled legal positions on the limited scope of interference.
respondent_arguments: The High Court was justified in exercising its revisional jurisdiction to set aside the charge framed by the Sessions Court.

cases.case_name: Amit Kapoor v. Ramesh Chander and Another
cases.principle: To explain the scope of Section 397 CrPC, clarifying that revisional jurisdiction can be invoked where the decisions under challenge are grossly erroneous, there is no compliance with the provisions of law, the finding recorded is based on no evidence, material evidence is ignored, or judicial discretion is exercised arbitrarily or perversely.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The revisional jurisdiction under Section 397 of the Code of Criminal Procedure is limited and intended to correct a patent defect or an error of jurisdiction or law. It can be invoked only in specific circumstances, such as when a challenged decision is grossly erroneous, there is non-compliance with legal provisions, a finding is based on no evidence, material evidence is ignored, or judicial discretion is exercised arbitrarily or perversely. A higher court should be reluctant to interfere with an order framing a charge unless the case substantially falls within these categories.
obiter: One of the inbuilt restrictions is that revisional jurisdiction should not be against an interim or interlocutory order.
The exercise of revisional jurisdiction itself should not lead to injustice ex facie.
Even framing of charge is a much advanced stage in the proceedings under the CrPC.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court committed a gross error by allowing a revision application that was legally untenable and setting aside the charge framed by the Sessions Court. The revision application was not maintainable because it was filed against an interlocutory order dismissing an application to modify a charge, which is expressly barred by Section 397(2) of the Cr.P.C. Furthermore, the underlying application for modification was itself a misuse of the legal process, as Section 216 of the Cr.P.C. does not grant an accused the right to seek discharge after a previous discharge application under Section 227 has already been dismissed.
legal_tests_applied: The scope of interference and exercise of revisional jurisdiction under Section 397 of the Cr.P.C. is extremely limited and should be exercised very sparingly. Revisional jurisdiction can be invoked only where the decision under challenge is grossly erroneous, there is non-compliance with the provisions of law, the finding recorded is based on no evidence, material evidence is ignored, or judicial discretion is exercised arbitrarily or perversely.
policy_considerations: The filing of fresh applications seeking discharge under the guise of Section 216 Cr.P.C., after a discharge application under Section 227 has been dismissed, is a practice used 'sometimes in ignorance of law and sometimes deliberately to delay the proceedings.'
When such untenable applications are filed, trial courts must decide them, leading to challenges in higher courts, which results in the 'whole criminal trial' getting 'derailed.'
This practice of filing frivolous and untenable applications to misuse the process of law is 'highly deplorable, and if followed, should be dealt with sternly by the courts.'

The imposition of costs on an accused who has 'sufficiently derailed the proceedings by filing frivolous and untenable applications one after the other' serves as a deterrent against such misuse of the legal process.
